p: Thank you. Next.

Good afternoon. Thank you to the Committees on Public Safety and Small Business, and Chairs Feliz and Thomas-Henry for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Gina Mitchell. I'm the Attorney-in-Charge of Law Reform and Policy at Brooklyn Defender Services in the

Queen's office. As public defenders, we routinely see the people we represent being arrested for taking food items, deodorant, toothbrushes, diapers, other basic necessities. While the media has sensationalized this issue, the vast majority of people arrested for retail theft are living in poverty and navigating complex issues, including serious mental illnesses, substance abuse problems and chronic housing instability. These problems demand nuanced and holistic solutions. In Queens and Brooklyn, we routinely see the issuing of trespass notices to people because they've been arrested for shoplifting or petty larceny. This means, as we've heard today, that if a person just enters a location where they were previously arrested for retail theft, even if it's because they can't afford food, they may face felony charges. For example, we represent one person who is chronically unhoused, navigating a complex physical illness and serious mental health concerns. She was arrested for taking hygiene items from a store and given one of these trespass notices. A few months later, she was arrested again for taking basic necessities. While she urgently needs

supportive housing and access to healthcare, she is now facing a prison sentence and the collateral consequences of criminal legal system involvement. We respectfully oppose Intro. 553 and Intro. 623, which would increase community surveillance and collaboration with the NYPD. These systems do not address the social issues and the affordability crisis in the city that leads to the vast majority of these cases. Instead, NYPD cameras means communities that are already heavily policed will have more data entered into NYPD's surveillance matrix, and I share the concerns of my colleagues on this panel. We recognize the need to support small businesses, and we urge the City to invest in services that meet the needs of people in our communities, rather than expanding reliance on policing, surveillance, and criminalization to solve these issues. We are urging you to look to real solutions, such as streamlining access to benefits so people can get the support to meet their basic needs, increasing job training programs and employment opportunities, particularly for young people, and pass a resolution in support of the New York State

Treatment Court Expansion Act, which will enable people to get access to critical mental health and substance use treatment. Thank you for the opportunity to testify, and I welcome any questions.
Can you repeat that last recommendation, the New York State?
To pass a resolution in support of the New York State Treatment Court Expansion Act, which is a bill that will enable people to get access to critical mental health and substance use treatment.

Thank you. You brought up a great point, and you gave some recommendations. That was going to be my question, in terms of how to alleviate increased retail theft for those who are in need, most specifically. Of everyone who has just testified, are there any other recommendations that we can do as a Council to help those individuals specifically?

Your Honor, we'll certainly address that in more detail in our written testimony. We need programs that address the nuanced

needs of our clients. There is a paucity and a lack of availability of suitable programs that are truly clinical, therapeutic, and community-based. Often, prosecutors are gatekeepers, and this can result in increased criminalization, increased trends towards enforcement, penalization, and higher jail sentences. We definitely need more access to programs that are truly tailored to helping our clients.
In your opinion, in the meantime, how do we also protect the business owners who are victims of the retail theft crimes?

In my opinion, the majority of clients that I work with are experiencing a complex range of needs. I truly think that we need to treat them as people. We've heard a lot of discussion today about numbers, and we really need to bring this back to the people who are involved. We are not going to police our way out of this. We're not going to surveil our way out of this. We need to actually address the problems that people and New Yorkers are facing in their lives.

I do fully agree with that. I will just add that in the particular context of retail theft, I think it's telling that while this bill, the Intro. 623, does mention plexiglass briefly and also sort of vaguely refers to other methods, a lot of the focus is on surveillance cameras because that's what's in the bill, and that's what's easy to put up and implement, especially for the NYPD who's not actually doing it but then can later use that footage to arrest our clients. I think thinking about the actual problem of retail theft, all of the other ways that the problem could be addressed in ways that would also actually help the small businesses with the affordability crisis, funding to hire more employees who can help in all ways with the store, including monitoring what's going on to some extent, things that don't involve a camera that someone is then either going to be monitoring in real time or afterwards laying over the spatial recognition technology on top of it. I think there are many more ways to think about layouts of the stores, all different ways of arranging things that don't involve this type of surveillance.
And do you guys keep stats on clients who are arrested for retail theft based on needs versus just kids being kids or large racket retail theft operations?

Our office does not. However, anecdotally, the professional experience of attorneys in my office is that the vast majority of cases do not fall into the category of these complex organized criminal enterprises, and the majority of anecdotal cases that were reported to me from attorneys who in particular have had clients issue the trespass notices related to people with the sorts of complex needs that we've been discussing.

I also do not have that information. I'll just mention that one of the other issues with Intro. 623 is that it has that language of crimes associated with retail theft without really explaining what that means. We heard a list of crimes that are sort of most often linked to that, but I think it's another way that the discretion to implement this program is really broad in the bill and concerning just given all the ways that it could

be weaponized and placed into communities of color, low-income communities, immigrant communities.
Thank you. Chair Feliz. Anything?
No questions.

Thank you, panel. We will now turn to virtual panelists. For virtual panelists, once your name is called, a Member of our Staff will unmute you, and the Sergeant-at-Arms will set the timer and give you the go-ahead to begin. Please wait for the Sergeant to announce that you may begin before delivering your testimony. Now, I will call our first virtual panelist. We have Pedro Suarez and Tonisha Hurd in that order.
Starting time.
Pedro, you may begin.

Thank you. My name is Pedro Suarez, the Executive Director of the Third Avenue Business Improvement District in the South Bronx

neighborhoods of Melrose and Mott Haven. We are one of the city's oldest and most heavily trafficked commercial districts. Regarding retail theft, I have observed too many incidents in the South Bronx go unreported because business owners, employees, and the general public seriously doubt whether individuals will be held accountable. We work closely with the 40th precinct to facilitate stronger relationships between local businesses and law enforcement. Last year, we worked closely with retailers like the Children's Place to ensure that security camera footage and details were shared with NYPD, which provided sufficient evidence to hold the offender accountable. Much of the retail theft that occurs on Third Avenue connects with substance abuse and mental health issues. Some individuals struggling with severe issues sometimes resort to retail theft to fund their addiction, repay informal debts, or as a cry for help. It is an unfortunate reality. The BID is installing additional security cameras to increase safety in the district because it is a known effective strategy for catching offenders around

various crimes. Last year, for example, video footage obtained from a local business helped apprehend a suspect who sexually assaulted another individual. We must be able to view these issues through multiple lens. While security cameras are not the only strategy, we cannot ignore that businesses in many low-income neighborhoods do not leverage security camera footage consistently. These are tools that are underutilized by businesses in the South Bronx, and we must be able to navigate a delicate balance between security and privacy. Small businesses in high-crime areas are reaching their breaking point. They are frustrated that retail theft is not taking as seriously as it should be, forcing business owners to eat the losses. Communities like the South Bronx lose shoppers when they witness shoplifting or when merchandise is inconveniently locked away. We can do better. City officials seeking additional data should engage with industry associations like the National Retail Federation, which released a report last year on retail theft. In closing, while I agree that retail theft often stems from larger issues, that shouldn't

prevent us from taking reasonable precautions. We live in an increasingly digital world, which demands that we work to improve digital security rather than avoid it altogether. Thank you for your time on this critical issue.
Thank you. Next up, we'll have Tonisha Hurd.
Starting time.
You may begin.

Good afternoon, and thank you so much to Chair Feliz and Chair Thomas-Henry and to the Members of the Committee on Public Safety and Small Business. My name is Tonisha Hurd, and I am representing Lisa Sorin, President of the Bronx Chamber of Commerce. We serve as the primary advocate for thousands of entrepreneurs who keep the Bronx moving, many of whom are first-generation owners operating on the front lines of our local economy. Today, our small businesses are facing a perfect storm, where they are battling tight margins while simultaneously acting as the primary targets of organized retail theft. For a small mom-and-pop shop

in the Bronx, the cost of a single major theft or high price of a modern security system isn't just a line item. It's a threat to their survival. And the Bronx Chamber of Commerce fully supports Intro. 553 and Intro. 623 because they offer practical and immediate relief. Intro. 553 bridges the affordability gap. It provides the financial assistance necessary for owners to install high-quality cameras and protective barriers and security measures that should be standard and not a luxury. Intro. 623 is equally vital because it creates a targeted pilot program in high-theft areas. The City is ensuring that resources reach the most vulnerable corridors first. We particularly value that data reporting requirement, which will prove exactly how these investments stabilize our neighborhoods. When we protect a storefront in the Bronx, we are not just protecting inventory. We are protecting jobs, families, and the safety of the residents who shop there. These bills move us from reactive policing to proactive prevention.

So, on behalf of the Bronx Chamber of Commerce, I urge the Council to pass both Intro. 553 and 623, and thank you all for your leadership on this issue and for the opportunity to testify.
Thank you for your testimony. Last, we have Christopher Leon Johnson.
Starting time.
You may begin.

Hello. My name is Christopher Leon Johnson. I support both bills. But City Council, this is the problem with retail theft, is that the majority of the people that commit these retail thefts are African-American, and we got the Working Families Party and many other organizations like CCA in Brooklyn, New York, and a lot of these non-profits that will be opposed to these bills because they need these people out there to commit these crimes because that's how they justify doing these little crappy rallies and press conferences and saying that, oh, we need to increase bail reform and increase to where people can commit

crimes as much as possible and go with straight impunity. I believe that the City Council, I think that the problem is like preventing the State is that the State Assembly is really captive to the Working Families Party that supports this stuff, that supports the crime. I appreciate Louis and Banks for introducing the 623 because they know who's really committing these crimes in the city when it comes to retail theft. Like I said, there's many, many Black people. I'm Black. I can say that. And what happens is that these small business owners, they get hurt. They get hurt daily. If they lose one thing, that could really shut down their business. I know that the City Council, like you, Ms. Henry, and Mr. Feliz, cares about this stuff, but you guys are in the minority when it comes to the mass majority, when it comes to a progressive caucus. The progressive caucus will be the main adversaries of making sure that these bills don't go through. I'll make this clear that when it comes to panic buttons, it's really needed. We need those panic buttons in these stores. When it comes to cameras, we need these cameras, and especially these

small stores. I think that the cameras should be prioritized to every small independent mom-and-pop grocery store and mom-and-pop retail business. But the problem, like I said, of course, the Legal Aid Society, the Brooklyn Defenders, and all these, STOP, they'll be against it because if you get arrested for shoplifting, if there's no cameras, and everybody knows about discovery, if there's no cameras with discovery, the case gets dropped. So, of course, they're going to be opposed to cameras because if they get a client, they know that the way that a case can get dropped is by having no cameras because they know that these days when it comes to eyewitnesses, they could be discredited. They on psychosis pills or they take a certain medication or they got a language barrier, they could easily be discredited. But like I said, I heard the testimony from the Bodega's people, and I hope on Tuesday and Friday they call out the real reason this stuff is happening because of a certain demographic that is doing these retail crimes and the Working Families Party and the progressives and the socialists, their supporters. And I'm going to say this right now, that

our Mayor, Zohran Mamdani, once infamously said that crime is a social construct. So, of course, he's going to be, if this bill ever gets to the floor, to the Mayor's desk, he's going to veto it. He wants this to keep on happening because it justifies the budgets of the NYPD. He's in hot water with Jessica Tisch, and he had to justify it. He would (TIMER CHIME) say, oh, this is not, we can't afford it…
Your time is expired.
Well, if they could afford giving 50 million dollars to the deliveristas…
Mr. Johnson, thank you.
He can give 50 million dollars to the…
Your time has expired.
To the… to these corrupt…
Mr. Johnson. Mr. Johnson.
Yeah.

Testing, testing. This is a microphone check for the New York City Council Committee on Civil and Human Rights. Today’s date is February 26th, 2026. This is being recorded in Hearing Room 1, 250 Broadway, and this is being recorded by Sergeant Ben Levy.

Good morning. Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Civil and Human Rights. Please silence all cell phone electronic devices. Moving forward, no one is to approach the dais. Chair, we are ready to begin.

Thank you. [GAVEL] Good morning, everyone. I'm Council Member Sandy Nurse, and I serve as Chair to the Committee on Civil and Human Rights. This is my first hearing as Chair for this Committee, so I first want to thank our wonderful Committee Staff who were here at City Hall very late last night for helping me to get into shape on all things Civil and Human Rights Committee, and also thank you to my deputy chief of staff, Fran, who is here supporting me as well. We are here with Council Members Lynn Schulman, Crystal Hudson, and I saw Shaun Abreu around.

I wanna congratulate you, Commissioner, on your appointment, and looking forward to working with you and nice to meet you, Deputy Commissioner Negash. Negash, I got it right? Okay. Also looking forward to the discussion later with the Commission on Racial Equity with Executive Director Linda Tigani, and we'll hear also later from Logan Clark from the New York City Independent Budget Office. So to everyone else in the room, thank you for being here. Nice to meet you all. The Carter Reforms of 2022 established a biennial cycle of racial equity planning and reporting in conjunction with the city's budgeting— budget planning process. This process is intended to connect racial equity commitments to quantifiable outcome-oriented metrics, including resource allocation and consistent monitoring. In addition, the Mayor and the Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice, also known as MOREJ, must issue a cost of living measure each year by March 31st. This measure is intended to provide a more realistic assess— estimate of the cost of living in New York City compared to traditional cost of living measures, so as to enable the finalized city budget

to more accurately account for New Yorkers' actual needs and struggles. Unfortunately, no racial equity plans or progress reports have ever been issued. In my opinion, it is one of the biggest failures of the Adams Administration that he did not prioritize and produce these plans. The Commission on Racial Equity, or CORE, cannot fully perform its charter mandate without a comprehensive, transparent, and measurable set of REPs to evaluate. These Charter Reforms are intended to promote transparency and accountability for city government, and in not issuing them in a timely manner, we risk further damaging the trust the people of New York have in their government. While I recognize that the timing of this hearing means we are hearing from a brand new administration with new appointments which has inherited the delays of the previous one, the Adams Administration's failure to comply with the Charter must not prevent a transparent examination of the city's budget preparations and negotiations for this year's budget. Today, this Committee will be looking for an update from MOERJ on its progress in bringing the city into compliance with the Charter. The city has

been working on these plans for a while now, and there should be plenty of action items and recommendations that can be discussed today. Sharing this information is key to the transparency and accountability that are at the heart of the racial equity planning process. I also look forward to hearing from CORE about its plans and capacity to evaluate the fiscal year 2027 budget with or without access to the city's racial equity plans and true cost of living metric. I'm hoping we can have a productive and meaningful conversation about the progress and challenges of this process to better understand how we can work toward a more equitable city. I want to reiterate that I'm looking forward to working with everyone in this room. The goal is to get the plans. The goal is to achieve racial equity. I hope you can see the Council as a partner on this and as a body to share in the problem solving where we have challenges. And I will now pass it to Committee Counsel to administer the oath.

Good morning. Could you please raise your right hands? Do you swear to tell

the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth today before this Committee?
Yes.
Oh, sorry. Yes.
Thank you very much. You may begin.

Good morning Chair Nurse, Members of the Committees on Civil and Human Rights, Members of the Council, and the public. My name is Afua Atta-Mensah. Thank you. And I serve as New York City's Chief Equity Officer and Commissioner of the Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice. I am pleased to be joined by Debash Nagash, Deputy Commissioner, and other members of the MOERJ team. Thank you for providing me the opportunity to speak before this Committee today to properly introduce myself, and to provide insight and information about the work of the Office of Equity and Racial Justice. You know, prior to serving in this role, I had the privilege of working with and on behalf of low-income New Yorkers as an attorney with the Legal Aid Society and with other legal services providers. Thereafter, I worked for Community Voices Heard,

leading its efforts to build the power of communities of color across New York, before going on to serve as the Chief of Programs for Community Change, a national power-building institution that provides campaign advocacy, electoral, and policy support to grassroots organizations across the country. Most importantly, I am a New Yorker who believes deeply in the transformative power of individuals who come together for their communities, and I am committed to building a just and equitable New York. I think it is important to provide some background on the Office of Equity and Racial Justice, which was established as the city's centralized office that takes on an intersectional approach to advance equity across our city. Our mandate is rooted in a simple but powerful belief that every New Yorker deserves the opportunity to live, work, and thrive with dignity. To realize that vision, MOERJ brings together several key initiatives and offices that work across government to tackle inequities experienced by communities in our city using various strategies from policy and research to advocacy and programs, including the Commission on Gender Equity, which

works to ensure our city leads in the development and implementation of best practices in gender equitable policies and programs. With a focus on economic mobility, health, and safety. The NYC Unity Project, which works to address inequities amongst LGBTQ New Yorkers, particularly youth, people of color, and TGN CNB people, as well as the New York Men's Initiative and NYC Her Future, sibling offices focused on addressing inequities among young men of color and young women of color respectfully— er, respectively— in education, employment, health, and justice. Our existence as an office is one that was guided by the will of the people of the city. New Yorkers overwhelmingly voted to embed racial equity and justice in our city's charter, which included documenting a vision and outlining a statement of values to guide how we carry out the work of government and serve the people, establishing the infrastructure to advance equity, including the creation of our office and the Commission on Racial Equity, as well as development of the— of New York City's first citywide racial equity plan. Plan and

ensuring we not only measure what it costs to meet basic needs but to live with dignity in our city. The previously mentioned foundational values in the preamble of the City Charter have served as the office's compass and urges all in government to justly value all talents and contributions, ensure the conditions for thriving for every person, and embrace vigilance, remedy, and reconstruction. As the office charged with implementing these mandates, our team has continued to translate our values into action and uplift these mandates with an eye towards transforming government. As I shared, an important part of the office's work is developing and implementing the Citywide Racial Equity plan, including individual agency uh, racial equity plans every 2 years and progress reports during off years. According to our Charter, the city's plan should include short and long-term goals, outcome measures, and strategies to reduce racial disparities. The Commission on Racial Equity works to ensure community voice is integrated into the planning process, sharing community equity priorities and outcome indicators to inform the plan as it is crafted.

The MOERJ team designed a planning process aimed at moving government towards equity and justice together. This was not designed as a compliance exercise, rather a unique opportunity for our city to work together longer— work together toward longer-term transformation. Over 40 agencies and 200+ staff were engaged in the process, and they were asked to review their priorities relative to the foundational values of the Charter, assess disparity data and community equity priorities, and commute— create short, midterm, and long-term goals and strategies that are responsive. The office supported agencies throughout the process of developing plans, leading full-day training workshops developing planning tools to guide the process, providing continuous support throughout the process, including dedicated office hours and one-on-one technical assistance. As a living and active plan, we aim to continue working together with city agencies and all stakeholders to upend the ways in which structural racism impacts our city. Now, prior to embarking on the citywide racial equity planning process, process that I previously

described, the office set up a framework to guide the planning process and work to understand and build on existing equity work across the city, explore the approaches, successes, and challenges of other localities advancing equity, including Philadelphia, Dallas, and, and Chicago, and launch an Advisory Board to guide the implementation of the Racial Justice Charter Amendments, focusing on the Citywide Racial Equity plan. The board convened over a dozen members, including local nonprofit leaders, civil rights trailblazers, and former government leaders who understand municipal operations. With that guidance and support, the office was committed to building the strategic framework necessary to not only advance equity but support structural reform. This required the office to ensure the framework addressed the core levers of government so the plan is sustainable. This meant centering things like service delivery, staffing, contracting, and budgeting from inception. This required integrating these core levers into the process and with regards to budgeting, working with agencies to consider if and how they allocate funds in their budget to remedy

disinvestment and past harm as they contemplated how to approach their agency's plan and begin to develop it. This can mean reallocating funds to meet the needs of historically marginalized communities, expanding services in key neighborhoods, experiencing longstanding disparities, and more. Given this is a living process and we will continue to refine and add to work, MOERJ has also continued to engage in equity and budgeting discussions over the last year, including discussions with academic institutions like the New School on the development and implementation of equity and budgeting tools, as well as attending and participating in two events in 2025 co-hosted by the New School Institute on Race, Power, and Political Economy, and the NYC Commission on Racial Equity. As we continue moving this process forward, we are committed to collaborating with our budget colleagues to integrate racial equity into the budgeting process by continuing to move city agencies to center equity in their own budget planning and decision-making, as new needs are just a fraction of the budget, and working with our City's Budget Office

to review agency requests with a lens that evaluates if and how proposals advance equity. As the Mayor shared on his 15th day in office, our Administration is committed to releasing the city's first Preliminary Racial Equity plan during his first 100 days in office. We look forward to releasing the Preliminary plan, finalizing it with the input of the public, as well as collaborating with our agency partners on implementation, the measuring of progress, and continuous improvements to eliminate racial disparities. As a city leader, 3 weeks into my role, I am learning a lot about this office and its current work. I also recognize this is a living plan and the first release is preliminary, so there will be more opportunity to make updates, including between the publication of the prelim plan and the final plan, which consists of a period for community feedback. Chair Nurse, I want to thank you for providing this space for this discussion, and I welcome any questions you or Council Members may have.

Thank you so much, Commissioner. I'm also learning about your agency, so

we're going to do this together. We're just going to start right off the bat, and if any Council Members have questions, just let me know. We'll throw you on the list. The previous Administration, as we've said now, we know they, they have failed to produce the plans, but They did draft a complete Preliminary Racial Equity plan. They cited that the City's Law Department as an impediment to releasing it. We're thankful that the Mayor plans to release it soon. We're looking forward to that. We understand the prior delays and setbacks are tied to the previous Administration. Can you er, you know, give us more insight into what obstacles remain to its immediate release? So that the public can begin to provide feedback?

Uh, thank you for the question. I, I would frame it this way. There are new leaders coming into the Administration every day, and part and parcel of what we are doing in meeting the Mayor's mandate of ensuring this comes out within his first 100 days is providing briefings and educating these new leaders, as the staff in their agencies had

already been part and parcel of our plan to, to create the, the plans for the individual agencies. So we are taking this time to brief leaders so that they are ready to move forward with their team in implementation. We fully expect that we will have this plan out within the 100-day period.

And so you— just to, to dive in a little bit more, you, you've all looked at it, the document. Do you— what, what can you say about it? I mean, is it, is it terrible? Is it, is it something that is in shape? I mean, could you just give us a little more insight into what you— and, and if the Law Department is the issue, can, can we hear a little bit more about what their concerns would be?

Again, I thank you for the question. Let me frame it this way as well. I'm, I'm— I think framing is important. This is a continuation. It's living and breathing. So I have seen aspects of the plan as each agency is, is in finalization and as we brief leaders. There are larger pieces of the federal landscape that have raised issues on on equity. We are lucky that in the City of New York, our Charter is clear and that we have a mandate that

we, we intend to abide by, and a Mayor who has made clear that is his intention. So we are moving forward with all deliberate speed, and I would frame that this plan is the first. It is preliminary. It is a work in progress, and, and it is our intention to have a start and to be a part of making this better. So it is an initial plan, and we're going to continue to make progress. I want to just provide some space for my deputy to add further.

Yeah, thank you, Commissioner. I would just also add, you know, the Commissioner mentioned, you know, 200 staff across 40-plus agencies that have been working on this plan. These are folks who have spent a lot of time doing equity work within their agency. These are folks who have worked across multiple Administrations. They're the people on the ground doing the real work, and those are the people that have really shaped this plan and, and continue to shape it with new leadership and staff coming on board.

Okay we can dive further into the plan in a little bit, but I do think understanding what the legal issues would be or what the Law Department's concerns would be would be

helpful. You know, we want to be partners in that and we want to share in the problem. Sometimes we have problems with the Law Department too. So you know, it, it's helpful to clue us in. To your knowledge, what efforts have been undertaken so far to address the community equity priorities, even in the absence of Citywide Racial Equity plans?

Thank you for that question. So I would mention two things here. I think number one when we began the racial equity planning process in 2024 we intentionally ensured that the draft equity pri— the community equity priorities, which at the time were draft, were integrated into the assessment process with agencies. So they were reviewing being briefed by the Commission on racial equity ahead of developing their plans. So we've really ensured that that's been integrated from the start. We're continuing to also look at the final priorities which were published to really see, particularly under this Administration, how we can integrate that into some of our other work, whether it be the Racial Equity plan itself or program investments.

Okay, uhm can you just talk a little bit more about what integrating means? Uhm, it's very broad uhm in terms of how that's filtering down into agency - uh what the agencies put forward when they're putting forward their pieces of the Preliminary budget.

Yeah, so let me speak to the planning process first, just because, you know, the Commissioner mentioned budgeting and equity and some of these other core levers of government were integrated into the process rather than treated as separate pieces. In the beginning of the planning process prior to starting to draft any plans we asked agencies to really look at a few things to ensure that prior to even drafting any ideas and outline for their plans that they're considering some key pieces of information. And one of those things is the draft equity community equity priorities. So prior to putting ideas to paper, making sure that they understand these are things that need to inform their plans, before they're drafted and community equity priorities were one of those things, along with

several other items we included during the assessment phase.
And do you think over the last year, for example, in the last cycle do you feel like those were integrated into what people put forward into their Preliminary Budgets?

I think they were inter— yeah, I think they were integrated into commu— er, excuse me, Preliminary Racial Equity plans. We also made an effort to ensure that agencies were sharing with us where community equity priorities aligned with the goals within their plan to really ensure that we were doing our part to, to hold our agencies and, and ourselves accountable.
Okay. Despite uh- you kind of answered this. To your knowledge, what kind of staffing or infrastructure do city agencies currently have for engaging in the Racial Equity planning process?

Yeah, I, I would— thank you for the question. At the beginning of the Racial Equity Planning process, we intentionally made an effort to ensure that every agency formed a racial equity planning team. We provided some criteria as well as

they crafted and, and pulled those teams together, ensuring that they are diverse, ensuring that they cut across different divisions of the agency so that equity work isn't sitting with one particular team or person. Uhm and then we've continued to— and we, we will continue to do so under our current Administration to refresh those teams, bring new people in. And so those are the folks who have led the process within their agencies to dra— craft their plans.
